frase_inicial: Timothy and Melanie: protecting Liam and Josh and cutting the expensive card interest are the two things that decide how your plan plays out

tarjetas.frente: High-rate credit card is holding the score back
tarjetas.reverso: Carrying that card at a high interest rate eats money every month and stops your household from showing stronger financial health. Paying it down frees room to insure the family and raises your published score.
tarjetas.detalle: Pay $6,800 from cash to the 18% card, leaving $11,200 balance on the card after the move.

tarjetas.frente: Both of you lack enough life insurance for the kids
tarjetas.reverso: If one of you dies, the children would lose a big share of household income while debts and future college costs remain. Adding cover protects Liam and Josh and clears a cap on the score once the card is addressed.
tarjetas.detalle: Add $235,000 of life cover to reach $485,000 total; plan models $491,800 needed after card paydown.

tarjetas.frente: No umbrella liability policy leaves assets exposed
tarjetas.reverso: Your home, cars and cash could be at risk from a large claim. An umbrella policy is a separate shield that keeps the money you’re saving for the kids out of someone else’s claim.
tarjetas.detalle: Add $1,000,000 umbrella to fill the shown gap; no umbrella is recorded today.

tarjetas.frente: You hold more cash than the emergency reserve needs
tarjetas.reverso: That extra cash is safe but mostly idle. It can be used to pay down the expensive card or buy protection without draining your cushion for emergencies.
tarjetas.detalle: Accessible cash today $150,800; cash above reserve and near-term goals $60,222.50.

tarjetas.frente: College saving for Liam and Josh is currently unfunded
tarjetas.reverso: No dedicated college accounts exist, so future tuition will compete with other priorities. Deciding how much of your spare cash and annual surplus to send there sets whether you need later loans or higher-year saving.
tarjetas.detalle: College funding gap $113,508.60; extra first-year saving needed $4,609.22.

tarjetas.frente: Retirement plan looks strong but depends on guaranteed income
tarjetas.reverso: Most retirement needs are covered by promised income sources. That’s good, but the plan depends on those holding up and on projected expenses being accurate in the years your cash flow dips.
tarjetas.detalle: Guaranteed income averages $171,055.83 per year; income covers 93% of retirement need.

tarjetas.frente: Your investable accounts are stock-heavy compared with Melanie’s comfort
tarjetas.reverso: The long-term accounts lean aggressive while Melanie prefers a steadier mix. That can make decisions harder and cause big swings you may later regret. Agreeing on how much swing you can accept matters.
tarjetas.detalle: Investable assets $210,000 with about 77% in stocks; household risk profiles differ.

tarjetas.frente: Monthly cash flow shows a surplus but the data is low confidence
tarjetas.reverso: The plan reports extra cash each year, but spending may be understated. Before redirecting surpluses, confirm real monthly spending so you don’t overcommit toward insurance or savings.
tarjetas.detalle: Net cash flow this year shown as $36,960.75; expense figures flagged low confidence.

tarjetas.frente: You’re collecting both employer matches—keep that going
tarjetas.reverso: Employer matching is free money for retirement. Maintain current retirement contributions while you decide how to use spare cash for insurance or card payoff.
tarjetas.detalle: Employer matches captured: $8,000 Timothy, $6,000 Melanie; current retirement saving steady.

tarjetas.frente: Order matters: money used for one goal is not available for others
tarjetas.reverso: Life insurance, umbrella, card payoff and college saving compete for the same spare cash. Choosing which to fund first changes which risks stay open and how your published score moves.
tarjetas.detalle: Plan models combined moves; card + life cover + umbrella raises score to 78 in scenario modeling.
